misconceptions.description: Assuming all points on a rotating rigid body have the same linear speed
misconceptions.trigger: learner states or computes equal linear speeds for points at different radii
misconceptions.feedback: Points on the same rigid body share angular velocity, not linear speed. Use v = r omega, so the point farther from the axis moves faster linearly.

misconceptions.description: Confusing tangential and normal acceleration roles
misconceptions.trigger: learner uses a_t = r omega^2 or a_n = r alpha
misconceptions.feedback: Tangential acceleration changes speed and uses alpha: a_t = r alpha. Normal acceleration changes direction and uses omega squared: a_n = r omega^2.

misconceptions.description: Using the wrong distance from the axis when applying v = r omega
misconceptions.trigger: learner measures r from an arbitrary point rather than the rotation axis
misconceptions.feedback: The radius in rigid-body kinematics is the perpendicular distance from the point to the rotation axis. Check the geometry before substituting into v = r omega.

misconceptions.description: Mixing angular and linear quantities as if they had the same meaning
misconceptions.trigger: learner adds omega directly to v or compares them without converting
misconceptions.feedback: Angular velocity and linear velocity are different physical quantities with different units. Use the geometry relation v = r omega when converting between them.
